section_summary: This section documents the worldwide transfer, examination, storage, and financial administration of former Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property after the war. Major files concern Japanese records in Beirut, Cairo, Havana, Mexico City, Bogotá, Santiago, Panama, Rome, and Vatican City, including inventories, intelligence assessments, inter-Allied custody agreements, trust accounts, and proposed sales of furniture. The surviving records were generally judged fragmentary or of limited intelligence value, although the Beirut files contained studies by Takashi Hayashi and a visa blacklist, while Havana’s records identified several potentially noteworthy Japanese residents.

subfiles.title: Department telegram on Japanese official and private property
subfiles.to: American diplomatic representative at Vatican City, Rome
subfiles.about: Instructions governing storage, sale, and financial administration of former Japanese diplomatic property.
subfiles.summary: The Department sees no objection to the proposed procedure and favors storing Japanese official property unless costs make storage impracticable. Official and private funds, including sale proceeds, are to be placed in a jointly controlled Allied trust account, with withdrawals permitted for custody expenses and limited relief to indigent Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Airgram reporting no Japanese mission in Honduras
subfiles.about: Honduras reports that it cannot supply the requested Japanese-property report because no Japanese diplomatic mission existed there.
subfiles.summary: The airgram answers the Department’s secret circular concerning property of Japanese diplomatic missions. It states that there had been no Japanese diplomatic mission in Honduras, so the requested reports could not be made.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary San José report on Japanese property
subfiles.about: A badly degraded Embassy record concerning former Japanese diplomatic property in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text identifies the U.S. Embassy at San José, Costa Rica, and refers to Japanese 'property.' Most of the substantive body and signature are lost in the OCR, although the page appears to belong to the series of mission replies to the Department’s property inquiry.

subfiles.title: Referral of British aide-mémoire on access to archives in Japan
subfiles.about: Referral of a British request concerning access to records and archives in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites a Departmental regulation centralizing responsibility for German, Italian-Fascist, and Japanese archives in FC. It forwards a British Embassy aide-mémoire of October 12, 1945, on British access to Japanese records, which had been held pending since November.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1085: Documents in Japanese Language Discovered in Files of Former Japanese Consulate in Beirut
subfiles.from: Gordon H. Mattison, U.S. Legation, Beirut
subfiles.about: Transmission of Alfred Regensburger’s examination of Japanese-language records from the former Beirut consulate.
subfiles.summary: Mattison reports that Alfred Regensburger, a Japanese-language expert and former British censorship reader, examined all Japanese-language material between January 7 and 9. No additional information of particular interest was found, and further examination was considered unprofitable. The records were repacked and stored, while the Legation suggested eventual use of the Japanese books by its library, the Library of Congress, or other American libraries.

subfiles.title: Report of Japanese Translator on Records of Beirut Jap Consulate
subfiles.about: Detailed assessment of the surviving Japanese consular correspondence, Takashi Hayashi’s papers, and a visa blacklist.
subfiles.summary: Regensburger found that nearly all sensitive wartime records had probably been destroyed or removed, leaving mainly routine trade, cultural, statistical, propaganda, and press-reporting files. Takashi Hayashi’s papers contained extensive studies of Egypt and a travel diary covering cities across the Middle East. The report also identifies meetings with Riad Solh and Adil Arslan and reproduces a thirty-seven-entry Japanese visa blacklist dating from 1937.

subfiles.title: Handwritten routing notes on the Beirut records
subfiles.about: Brief internal notes asking that the Beirut material be retained temporarily and recording a promised callback.
subfiles.summary: One note asks 'Joe' to keep the material for a while in connection with Japanese work. A second says that Simpson will call back; the remaining handwriting is largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-29 on continued storage of Beirut consular property
subfiles.about: Instructions for storing or selling former Japanese consular property and controlling access to Japanese books.
subfiles.summary: The Department directs continued storage, allowing sale of non-archival movable effects only where deterioration, depreciation, or excessive cost makes storage impracticable. Sale proceeds and official funds are to enter a joint Allied trust account. Japanese books are to remain nominally Japanese property but may be stored where interested Allied mission personnel can use them under a control system.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1279: Relinquishment by the Swiss Government of Japanese Archives and Property in Egypt
subfiles.from: S. Pinkney Tuck, American Legation, Cairo
subfiles.about: Report on the Swiss transfer of Japanese official archives and property to the Four Powers and then to Egyptian guardianship.
subfiles.summary: Alfred Brunner transferred Japanese official archives, official furniture, officials’ personal property, and civilians’ property to representatives of China, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The Four Powers then placed the material under provisional Egyptian guardianship, administered by Mohamed Aly Sadek Bey, while retaining authority over its disposition. Furniture was expected to be sold, but sealed archives were to be examined and retained intact despite reports that most important records had been burned.

subfiles.title: Procès-verbal concerning Japanese official premises, furniture, and archives in Egypt
subfiles.from: Alfred Brunner, Swiss minister in Egypt
subfiles.to: B. C. Flynn, C. B. Lyon, P. M. Dneprov, and Chang Chi-Hsien
subfiles.about: Formal transfer of the former Japanese Legation and consular furniture and archives to the Allied representatives.
subfiles.summary: Brunner places the Japanese government’s furniture and archives at Cairo in the custody of the British, American, Soviet, and Chinese representatives. The instrument incorporates inventories for the Cairo Legation and the consulates at Alexandria and Port Said and records removal of the Swiss protective plaque.

subfiles.title: Procès-verbal concerning private property of Japanese diplomatic and consular agents
subfiles.from: Alfred Brunner, Swiss minister in Egypt
subfiles.to: Representatives of the United Kingdom, United States, Soviet Union, and China
subfiles.about: Formal transfer of private property belonging to former Japanese diplomatic and consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss minister consigns to the four Allied representatives private property belonging to Japanese diplomatic and consular agents and held in the former Cairo Legation. The parties certify that the previously supplied inventory had been checked and found accurate.

subfiles.title: Procès-verbal concerning private property of Japanese nationals
subfiles.from: Alfred Brunner, Swiss minister in Egypt
subfiles.to: Representatives of the United Kingdom, United States, Soviet Union, and China
subfiles.about: Formal transfer of private property belonging to Japanese civilians in Egypt.
subfiles.summary: Brunner transfers private property of Japanese nationals stored at the former Cairo Legation to the four Allied representatives. The instrument notes an attached recapitulatory valuation of the various sequestrated Japanese goods and confirms the prior inventory.

subfiles.title: Record of transfer to provisional Egyptian control and guardianship
subfiles.from: Representatives of China, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States
subfiles.to: Mohamed Aly Sadek Bey for the Egyptian Government
subfiles.about: Placement of Japanese archives and property under temporary Egyptian guardianship on behalf of the Four Powers.
subfiles.summary: The Allied representatives deliver the former Japanese Legation’s archives and property to Mohamed Aly Sadek Bey at the Zamalek residence. Egypt is to exercise provisional control in the name of the Four Powers, and the arrangement remains subject to revision by them. The record refers to the inventory signed on January 16 and prepared by the Swiss Legation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 925 transmitting report on Japanese Legation archives in Havana
subfiles.from: H. Bartlett Wells, U.S. Embassy, Havana
subfiles.about: Covering despatch for an Embassy report on the Japanese archives and property held in Havana.
subfiles.summary: Wells responds to the Department’s November 1945 circular directing a report on the takeover of Japanese diplomatic and consular records and property. He forwards an enclosed report and notes that copies were supplied to the military, naval, and legal attachés.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese Legation Archives and Property in Havana
subfiles.about: Assessment of Japanese registration cards, letters, maps, and office property held by the Cuban Ministry of State.
subfiles.summary: The Cuban Ministry of State held sealed boxes containing mainly furniture and insignificant papers, plus a card file on Japanese residents that was examined by Rafael Francisco Vidal y Madrazo and Pedro Anton García. The investigators identified several potentially noteworthy people, including Army officer Naoji Iwaki, Ekiko Ichihara, Foreign Office inspector Kiyoshi Uchiyama, and individuals expressly recalled under the New Order. Three letters and two maps were judged to have little value, and the Embassy concluded that the collection was almost entirely negligible for intelligence purposes.

subfiles.title: Contents of Safe
subfiles.about: Inventory of Japanese-language books, stamps, correspondence, press files, diplomatic telegrams, and other objects found in a safe associated with Iraq.
subfiles.summary: The inventory lists Japanese ledgers, receipt books, stamps, seals, a presentation box, press and radio files, accounts, diplomatic telegrams, payroll material, and Japanese political publications. It also mentions files on Iraqi affairs, the Rashid Ali rebellion, a Churchill speech, petroleum resources, and a letter from W. H. Boswall to Mr. Sakamoto.

subfiles.title: Letter to the British ambassador on Japanese funds in Chile
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard for the U.S. ambassador
subfiles.to: John Hurleston Leche, British ambassador in Chile
subfiles.about: Proposal to retain the existing Chilean arrangement for Japanese funds and Swedish protective expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Millard explains that the main Japanese funds are already held in trust on behalf of the Four Allied Powers. Because 304,544.18 Chilean pesos had separately been left with the Swedish Legation for routine protection of Japanese interests, he proposes that no additional access to the principal trust account be arranged.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 113 reporting the Cairo transfer
subfiles.about: Notice that the Swiss representative had transferred Japanese archives and property to the Four Powers, which placed them with the Egyptian Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Tuck reports completion of the Swiss transfer and the subsequent delivery of custody to the Egyptian Foreign Office. He states that a despatch will follow. Pages 560-561 contain largely illegible handwritten routing or follow-up notes associated with the telegram.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 27,994: Disposal of Japanese Archives
subfiles.from: Raymond H. Geist for the U.S. ambassador, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Urgent request for instructions on disposition of Japanese archives held by the Swedish Legation in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The Soviet Embassy was pressing for decisions on the Japanese archives, funds, and property, while British instructions suggested sending the archives to Washington for processing. Geist notes that the Department had supplied guidance on funds and property but not on the archives. He asks urgently for instructions because the British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives were ready to act.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Grigori Kasparov
subfiles.about: Discussion of Soviet proposals for Japanese assets, archives, rent, and payments to the Japanese Committee in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Kasparov said Moscow favored dividing all Japanese assets among the Four Powers and wished the Soviet Embassy to study the archives, whether in Mexico City or Washington. He objected to monthly payments of 8,300 pesos to a Japanese Committee and to continued rent for Japanese quarters, believing the expenditures potentially unfriendly to the Allies. Geist replied that the U.S. ambassador had repeatedly requested Department instructions and expected them shortly.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 625 transmitting Item No. 86 of the Panama archives inventory
subfiles.from: V. Lansing Collins Jr. for the U.S. ambassador, Panama
subfiles.about: Transmission of a carbon copy of a Japanese-language archival item requested by the Department.
subfiles.summary: Collins responds to the Department’s January 14 request for a photostatic copy of Item No. 86 from the inventory of surviving Japanese archives in Panama. He sends one of five carbon copies and states that it need not be returned.

subfiles.title: Copy of Item No. 86 from the Japanese archives in Panama
subfiles.about: A short Japanese or Chinese-character document preserved as Item No. 86 of the Panama inventory.
subfiles.summary: The page consists principally of East Asian characters and bears the enclosure notation for Despatch No. 625. The OCR does not yield a reliable translation or description of its substantive contents.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-33 reporting no Japanese funds in Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Report that no Japanese cash or liquid resources existed locally and that no action was required.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy refers to its earlier despatches and the Department’s circular on property of Japanese diplomatic missions. Because those records established the absence of cash or liquid resources, it reports that no action is being taken.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese documents captured in Rome
subfiles.from: Wade H. Coleman Jr., Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Offer to transfer Japanese documents captured at Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha premises in Rome before their disposal.
subfiles.summary: Naval Intelligence held Japanese documents captured by Allied forces after the fall of Rome, chiefly from Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha premises and possibly relevant to Safehaven investigations. Since the Navy no longer needed them, Coleman asks whether any State Department unit wants the material before disposal.

subfiles.title: State Department request for captured Rome documents
subfiles.from: Frederick B. Lyon, Department of State
subfiles.to: Wade H. Coleman Jr., Navy Department
subfiles.about: Request that the Navy provide State with the Japanese documents captured in Rome and any available index or summary.
subfiles.summary: Lyon accepts the Navy’s offer and asks that the captured Japanese documents be sent to the Department for review. He also requests any index or summary the Navy may have prepared.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Vatican City requesting expedited reply
subfiles.about: Request for an expedited response to an earlier Vatican City telegram.
subfiles.summary: Gowen states that he has been asked to expedite a reply to AMVAT telegram 241 of December 19. No further substantive description of the earlier matter is included.

subfiles.title: Messersmith letter seeking instructions on Mexican Japanese assets
subfiles.about: Private request for clear authority to negotiate with British, Soviet, and Chinese colleagues over Japanese archives and funds in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith opposes the Soviet proposal to divide Japanese assets and favors retaining the funds under the control of the four chiefs of mission. He agrees that the 8,300-peso monthly payment to the Japanese Committee should be carefully reviewed. He asks Carrigan to hasten instructions defining either specific limits or broad negotiating discretion.

subfiles.title: Department telegram rejecting division of Japanese funds in Mexico
subfiles.about: Department approval of Messersmith’s opposition to dividing Japanese funds and notice of a planned expert archival mission.
subfiles.summary: The Department fully agrees that the Japanese funds and property proceeds should not be divided and says its circular instructions will not be modified. It supports eliminating or sharply reducing Japanese Committee payments to the minimum justified need. An expert team is expected to examine the archives in Mexico City.

subfiles.title: Messersmith follow-up letter on Despatch No. 27,994
subfiles.about: Request that Messersmith’s fuller personal letter be considered with the formal despatch on Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith says Despatch No. 27,994 was incomplete and asks Carrigan to place his accompanying personal letter before the responsible Department officers. He reiterates that he needs either specific directives or full latitude in dealing with his three Allied colleagues.

subfiles.title: Carrigan acknowledgment to Messersmith
subfiles.about: Acknowledgment that Messersmith’s letter was added to the file and shown to the responsible officers.
subfiles.summary: Carrigan confirms receipt of Messersmith’s January 23 request and says the earlier letter has been brought to the attention of the officers handling Japanese archives. He hopes the recently issued circular airgram will assist the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 334: Possession Taken of Japanese Archives and Property in Colombia
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, U.S. Embassy, Bogotá
subfiles.about: Report on Allied acquisition, storage, and proposed disposal of Japanese archives, funds, furniture, and private property in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Wiley describes negotiations by the American, British, and Soviet missions with the Swiss chargé, who surrendered Japanese archives, property, and funds after Switzerland ended its protection of Japanese interests. The archives were sealed at the British residence, while 82,438.42 Colombian pesos awaited unfreezing and deposit under joint control. The Embassy planned a discreet public auction of ordinary furniture and a low-value private automobile, while preserving archives, pictures, vases, and possible personal effects.

subfiles.title: Wiley note requesting Swiss transfer of Japanese assets
subfiles.about: Four-Power request for the transfer of Japanese archives, property, and funds to joint Allied custody in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Wiley asks that all Japanese official and private archives, properties, and funds held by the Swiss Legation be transferred to the American, British, and Soviet missions pending arrival of a Chinese representative. He also asks Switzerland to continue protecting Japanese nationals if its government finds that convenient.

subfiles.title: Rossat reply agreeing to transfer Japanese assets
subfiles.about: Swiss acceptance of the requested inspection and transfer of former Japanese archives, property, and funds.
subfiles.summary: Rossat states that Swiss instructions authorize compliance with Wiley’s request. Inspection is scheduled for December 22 and formal transfer for December 27. He has not yet received a decision on continuing protection of Japanese nationals but promises to consult Bern.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Allied planning for the Bogotá transfer
subfiles.about: Record of American, British, and Soviet planning for custody and disposal of Japanese assets and archives.
subfiles.summary: The participants agree that Wiley will request the Swiss transfer and that a three-mission committee will manage the archives, furniture, and personal-property cases. They discuss discreet furniture sales, landlord claims, preservation of potentially valuable Japanese prints, and Soviet access to Japanese-language expertise. Wiley also plans to press for unblocking the official funds, while all expect Switzerland may end protection of Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Wiley memorandum of conversation with the Swiss chargé
subfiles.about: Discussion of the impending Japanese-asset transfer, safes, private property, and possible missing personal archives.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss chargé welcomes the proposed Four-Power transfer and describes the status of the former Legation building and its safes. Wiley suggests leaving the built-in safes with the landlord and selling a Japanese merchant’s automobile and other property into a blocked account. The Swiss chargé believes the former Japanese minister’s personal archives may have been entrusted to the gardener.

subfiles.title: Letter establishing joint account for Japanese funds
subfiles.from: Gerald A. Mokma for the U.S. ambassador
subfiles.to: National City Bank of New York, Bogotá
subfiles.about: Instructions for depositing 82,438.42 Colombian pesos under three-mission joint control.
subfiles.summary: Mokma deposits the former Japanese funds in an account held jointly by the British Embassy, Soviet Legation, and U.S. Embassy. No withdrawal may be made without one authorized signature from each of the three missions.

subfiles.title: Snow letter on storage and transfer arrangements
subfiles.about: British confirmation of arrangements for transferring and storing Japanese archives and personal effects in Bogotá.
subfiles.summary: Snow encloses his letter to the Colombian foreign minister and records the plan for the senior Allied representative to receive the Japanese archives, property, and funds from Rossat. He offers storage space at his Chapinero residence for the archives and five cases said to contain the former Japanese minister’s personal effects.

subfiles.title: Snow letter requesting unblocking of Japanese funds
subfiles.about: Request for Colombian action to unblock Japanese funds when the Swiss protecting power releases them.
subfiles.summary: Snow informs the foreign minister that Switzerland is prepared to transfer Japanese official archives, property, and funds to the American, Soviet, and British missions. He asks Colombia to unblock the funds promptly and promises that money needed for continued protection of Japanese nationals will remain available to the protecting power.

subfiles.title: Swiss note ending protection of Japanese interests in Colombia
subfiles.about: Notification that Switzerland will not continue protecting Japanese interests or nationals in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Rossat reports that the Swiss Confederation has declined to continue its protective role under the changed conditions. Switzerland therefore transfers not only the archives, property, and funds already assumed by the Allied missions but also full responsibility for Japanese interests in Colombia.

subfiles.title: Procès-verbal of the transfer of Japanese archives, property, and funds in Bogotá
subfiles.to: Gerald A. Mokma, Frank Collinge Ogden, and Simeon A. Gonionskii
subfiles.about: Formal record of Switzerland’s transfer of all Japanese assets in its custody to the American, British, and Soviet missions.
subfiles.summary: Rossat delivers the archives, household contents, an 82,438.42-peso check, safe keys and combinations, official emblem and flag, five personal-property cases, and other property belonging to Japanese nationals. The document explains that the archives could not be verified because they were sealed, labeled in kanji, and received without Swiss responsibility from the Spanish Legation.

subfiles.title: Inventory of Japanese Government furniture and effects in Bogotá
subfiles.to: American and British Embassies and Soviet Legation
subfiles.about: Room-by-room inventory of furniture, fixtures, office equipment, and household effects in the former Japanese Legation.
subfiles.summary: The inventory covers reception rooms, bedrooms, offices, archives, dining areas, kitchen, service rooms, and corridors throughout the former Legation. It lists furniture, carpets, curtains, safes, filing cabinets, artwork, a piano, radiola, ping-pong table, and Japanese fencing equipment. Several kitchen items remained in the charge of Tomás Tada.

subfiles.title: Archives of Japanese Legation
subfiles.about: Brief box-level description of the sealed archives of the former Japanese Legation in Bogotá.
subfiles.summary: The list describes six sealed boxes containing numbered files, miscellaneous books and papers, newspaper cuttings, twenty-four film rolls, office equipment, an atlas, and a large apparent dictionary. The boxes bore the seals of the American and British Embassies and the Soviet Legation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,397: Allocation of Japanese funds for protection of Japanese interests in Chile
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard for the U.S. ambassador, Santiago
subfiles.about: Report on the 304,544.18-peso allocation left with the Swedish Legation and the principal Allied trust account.
subfiles.summary: Millard reports that the principal Japanese cash and liquid resources were taken over in November 1945 and held for the Four Allied Powers. A separate 304,544.18 Chilean pesos remained with the Swedish Legation for routine protection of Japanese interests. The Embassy requested expenditure reports, while British and Chinese representatives agreed that Sweden did not need access to the larger trust account.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting Swedish accounting for Japanese protective funds
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard for the U.S. ambassador
subfiles.to: Tore Högstedt, Swedish chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Request for estimates and expenditure reports covering funds left with Sweden for routine Japanese-interest work.
subfiles.summary: Millard endorses the existing arrangement under which Sweden retained 304,544.18 Chilean pesos rather than receiving access to the main Allied trust account. He asks how long the money will last and requests reports for November-December 1945 and January-March 1946. Allowable expenses are limited to indigent relief, routine protecting-power costs, and moving or storing Japanese diplomatic property and archives.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Chinese minister on Japanese funds in Chile
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard for the U.S. ambassador
subfiles.to: Chaucer E. Wu, Chinese minister in Chile
subfiles.about: Request for Chinese concurrence in retaining the existing trust-account arrangement for Japanese funds.
subfiles.summary: Millard explains that the principal funds are held for the Four Allied Powers and that 304,544.18 Chilean pesos were left separately with the Swedish Legation. He proposes that Sweden receive no access to the main trust account unless the Chinese minister objects.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of letter to the British ambassador on Japanese funds
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard for the U.S. ambassador
subfiles.to: John Hurleston Leche, British ambassador in Chile
subfiles.about: A heavily degraded duplicate of the proposal to leave Swedish protective funds separate from the Allied trust account.
subfiles.summary: The page repeats the substance of the January 15 letter explaining the Allied trust account and the separate 304,544.18-peso Swedish allocation. Although the OCR is poor, it again proposes leaving the existing arrangement unchanged.

subfiles.title: British Embassy reply approving the Chilean funds arrangement
subfiles.about: British concurrence that Sweden need not access the main Japanese trust account while its separate allocation remains available.
subfiles.summary: Leche calls the arrangement entirely satisfactory and agrees that Swedish access and accountability are unnecessary until the money already left with Sweden is exhausted. He has forwarded copies of the correspondence to the Foreign Office and British Embassy in Washington.

subfiles.title: Chinese Legation reply approving the Chilean funds arrangement
subfiles.from: Tang Wu for the Chinese minister
subfiles.about: Chinese concurrence with the Allied trust account and separate Swedish allocation for protecting Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Tang Wu acknowledges the deposit of former Japanese cash and liquid resources in banks for the Four Allied Powers. He agrees that the Swedish chargé need not receive access to the main account because 304,544.18 Chilean pesos had already been left with Sweden for routine protection of Japanese citizens and interests in Chile.
